subtitle: read_* to load, to_* to save — Chapter 6 begins.

caption: A finance team exports a CSV, an analyst emails Excel, an application hands you JSON — same data, three shapes.

code:
orders.to_csv("orders.csv", index=False)
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
df.dtypes
# order_date  object   <- CSV has no date type!
caption: Without index=False, pandas writes row numbers as an extra unnamed column you didn't want.

eyebrow: Arguments that tame a messy CSV
caption: usecols picks columns, dtype sets types up front, parse_dates converts text to datetime, nrows peeks.
sep sets the delimiter, decimal="," reads 1,5 as 1.5, na_values adds extra strings that mean missing.

code:
orders.to_excel("orders.xlsx", sheet_name="Orders", index=False)

with pd.ExcelWriter("report.xlsx") as w:
    orders.to_excel(w, sheet_name="Orders", index=False)
    orders.describe().to_excel(w, sheet_name="Summary")
caption: Needs pip install openpyxl. sheet_name=None on read_excel returns a dict of DataFrames, one per sheet.
orient="records" gives a list of objects, the shape most web APIs use. Dates come back as plain text.

code:
pd.json_normalize(nested, record_path="items",
                   meta=["id", ["customer", "name"]])
#   sku  qty  id  customer.name
# 0  A1    2   1            Ana
caption: record_path expands a list into rows; meta copies parent fields onto each one.
